Old Windows reaches back to the earliest days of the graphical desktop, presenting your portfolio as a working vintage computer environment complete with application windows, retro navigation, and a workspace that feels genuinely pulled from a past era. The design leans into the utilitarian charm of early Windows — flat colours, blocky controls, and a no-frills layout that was purely practical. This theme suits developers who appreciate computing history and want their portfolio to reflect a deep, authentic connection to where software began.

## Theme Overview

Old Windows draws from the earliest iterations of the Windows graphical interface — pre-95 styling with flat, blocky window borders, simple menu bars, and a desktop workspace that prioritises function over decoration. Content is housed inside application-style windows that echo classic programs like File Manager, Notepad, and Program Manager. The colour palette is muted and utilitarian, dominated by grey, white, and the occasional splash of flat colour. Navigation mirrors the menu-driven logic of early Windows, guiding visitors through your work in an orderly, almost bureaucratic fashion that pays genuine homage to computing's graphical origins.

## Design Highlights

- Pre-Windows 95 aesthetic with flat borders, blocky window chrome, and minimal decoration
- Application-window content panels reminiscent of early Windows programs
- Menu-driven navigation echoing the interface conventions of classic desktop software
- Muted grey-and-white palette with utilitarian, function-first visual logic
- Authentic vintage workspace atmosphere rooted in early graphical computing history

## Who This Theme Suits

Old Windows is ideal for developers, engineers, and technical professionals with a genuine passion for computing history and legacy systems. It suits those working in low-level programming, systems architecture, or retro computing communities, and makes a strong impression on anyone who values depth of knowledge and a portfolio that reflects real technical heritage rather than surface-level nostalgia.
